content: Studies have shown that the use of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) during pregnancy significantly reduces maternal hepatitis B virus (HBV) DNA levels and the rate of failure of infant immunoprophylaxis. Observational studies have reported a 0% rate of mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HBV and favorable safety profiles for TDF. There are no significant safety concerns associated with the use of TDF or tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) during pregnancy. According to the Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry as of December 2022, there is no significant increase in the risk of birth defects in infants born to mothers who used TDF or TAF during any trimester of pregnancy. However, TAF has not yet been approved for the treatment of hepatitis B during pregnancy. For children and adolescents with chronic hepatitis B (CHB), both TDF (including dual-therapy regimens such as TDF + lamivudine [3TC] or TDF + emtricitabine [FTC]) and entecavir (ETV) have been shown to be effective. Data on TAF use in children are limited, but TAF may be a desirable option in the future due to concerns about bone toxicity associated with TDF. The European Medicines Agency (EMA) and the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) have approved TDF for children aged two years and older with CHB. The FDA has approved TAF for children aged 12 years and older with compensated liver disease, while the EMA has approved TAF for children aged six years and older who weigh more than 25 kg. However, as more adolescents begin treatment, the risk of TDF-related bone loss may become a growing concern, particularly for children and adolescents with developing bones. For individuals with renal insufficiency or osteoporosis, studies have demonstrated the benefits of switching from TDF to TAF, including improvements in creatinine clearance and bone mineral density in the hip and spine, although serum cholesterol levels may increase. Randomized trials comparing TAF and TDF in HIV monoinfection (excluding HBV coinfection) have shown that TAF has less negative impact on bone mineral density and renal function markers. Clinical events related to bone and renal health were rare with both drugs, and there was no difference in the rate of HIV viral load suppression. However, TAF was associated with greater increases in cholesterol levels and body weight. Pharmacological studies have shown acceptable plasma concentrations of TAF during pregnancy, but more data are needed to establish its safety in this population. Limited data are available on the use of TAF in children and adolescents, with safety and pharmacokinetic studies using adult dosing in weight bands above 25 kg. For children weighing 14 to less than 25 kg and older than two years, low-dose formulations of FTC + TAF (120/15 mg) with a boosted third agent have shown favorable bone and renal safety, viral load suppression, and tolerability. The 2015 WHO guidelines on hepatitis B care and treatment recommended antiviral therapy with nucleos(t)ide analogues with a high genetic barrier to resistance, such as TDF or ETV. ETV was recommended for children aged 2–11 years. For the 2024 updated guidelines, the use of TAF and dual therapy was considered as alternative antiviral regimens. TDF or ETV remains the preferred first-line regimen, with dual therapy as an alternative where access to TDF monotherapy is limited. TAF use is reserved for individuals with renal impairment, osteoporosis, or adolescents. All recommended nucleos(t)ide analogues (TDF, TDF + 3TC or FTC, ETV, and TAF) are potent inhibitors of HBV replication and effective in reducing disease progression. However, HBeAg seroconversion occurs in only 10–15% of HBeAg-positive individuals per year, and HBsAg loss is infrequent. These drugs have a high genetic barrier to resistance, with low observed rates of resistance over long-term follow-up. Resistance to ETV is more common in individuals with prior 3TC resistance, limiting its use in settings where 3TC has been widely prescribed. TAF is less widely available and more expensive than TDF, primarily due to its patent protection and lower demand. However, as TAF adoption increases, it is anticipated that its cost may decrease. For those with coinfection, dual NRTI inhibitors, including TDF with 3TC or FTC, are preferred. ETV is not suitable for individuals with both HIV and HBV. Discontinuation of HBV-active agents can lead to severe liver damage due to HBV reactivation, so patients should be advised against stopping these medications without medical supervision. Research gaps include the need for long-term studies comparing TAF and TDF on bone mineral density, lipids, weight, and other clinical outcomes, particularly in aging populations and low-resource settings. Cost-effectiveness studies on alternative regimens and the development of curative antiviral strategies for HBV are also needed. Injectable and implantable long-acting treatments for hepatitis B are under evaluation. For pregnant women, TDF prophylaxis is recommended to prevent MTCT of HBV in those with HBV DNA ≥200,000 IU/mL or positive HBeAg, starting from the second trimester until delivery or completion of the infant HBV vaccination series. In settings without access to HBV DNA or HBeAg testing, TDF prophylaxis may be considered for all HBsAg-positive pregnant women. All infants should receive a timely birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine, followed by completion of the primary immunization series.
